frase_gancho.texto: A priest dressed in the skin of a monster.

puente_narrativo.texto: The Olmec world appears again in the next display case, with a naked child who has a jaguar’s mouth. He has more in common with the priest than it seems.

guion_corto.texto: This hollow clay figure comes from Atlihuayan, in Morelos. He is a robust man, seated, with half-closed eyes, a mouth with downturned corners, and a head intentionally deformed. But what is extraordinary is what he wears: the complete skin of a fantastic being, whose head rests on his own and whose claws fall over his shoulders. Specialists read him as a priest transforming into the earth monster, which some see as a caiman and others as a jaguar. His style is Olmec, but he was made several hundred kilometers from the Gulf Coast: a sign that ideas traveled.

guion_largo.texto:
To reach Atlihuayan, you have to leave the Valley of Mexico and head south, down into the warm lands of Morelos, near Yautepec. Today it is an area of orchards. Three thousand years ago, it was one of the places where you could feel most strongly the style of a culture that was born far away, in the humid jungles of the Gulf Coast: the Olmec. A few kilometers away, in Chalcatzingo, there are even Olmec reliefs carved into the rock of a hill, with figures standing in the rain and fantastic animals.

The figure in front of you shows this clearly. He is a robust man, seated, with half-closed eyes and a mouth with downturned corners, the famous Olmec “feline mouth.” His head has the elongated shape achieved by molding the skull from infancy, the custom you saw in Hall 1. And over him, like a mantle, falls the skin of a fantastic animal: the monster’s head sits on top of his own, and the claws hang over his shoulders and chest, as if embracing him.

What is this animal? Here there is a debate. Some identify it as a celestial caiman; others, as a jaguar or as the “Olmec dragon,” a being that mixes features of the jaguar, the serpent, and the caiman. What matters is the idea: this figure does not put on a garment, he becomes another being. In Mesoamerica, wearing an animal’s skin was not a disguise, it was a transformation: whoever wore it shared in its strength and its spirit.

This idea appears again and again. Centuries later, Mexica warriors would dress in jaguar skins and eagle helmets to become those animals, and in the Mexica Hall you will see the head of an [Eagle Warrior](mna_s06_guerrero_aguila) emerging from the jaws of his helmet. And even today, in the upstairs halls, there are masks and ritual costumes with which people stop being themselves to embody a spirit during a festival.

The figure is also a technical feat. It is hollow, modeled in clay with thin walls, and it reaches almost thirty centimeters. For something like this to survive firing, the potter has to master the thickness of the clay and leave openings for the air. That it has come down to us intact says a great deal about the skill of whoever made it.

And here comes the big question that, for decades, has stirred archaeologists: were the Olmec the “mother culture” of Mesoamerica, as Alfonso Caso and Miguel Covarrubias thought, or a sister culture among many? A piece like this one, made in Morelos in a style that came from far away, shows that ideas, objects, and specialists traveled hundreds of kilometers. The full answer awaits you in the Gulf Coast Hall, where you will meet the Olmec in their own home.

texto: Look for the monster’s head on top of the priest’s head
Notice the claws that fall over his shoulders and chest
Observe the mouth with downturned corners and the half-closed eyes

texto.Culture: Preclassic of the Central Highlands, with Olmec influence

texto.pregunta: Myth: The Priest of Atlihuayan is a warrior disguised as a jaguar to go into battle.
texto.respuesta: Reality: He is a ritual figure who transforms into a fantastic being, an earth monster in the Olmec style; it is not a war disguise.
